title: Diodes and rectifiers
goals: Say which way a diode conducts, and test one with a meter
Work out the DC a half-wave or bridge rectifier gives from an AC supply
Size the series resistor for an LED or a zener
Estimate the ripple left after a smoothing capacitor
Say why a DC relay coil has a diode across it, and which way round
summary:
A **diode** lets current through one way only, like a check valve. Current flows from the **anode** to the **cathode** (the end with the **band**).

- **Forward biased** (anode more positive): it conducts once past its forward voltage, about **0.6–0.7 V** for silicon (0.2–0.4 V for a Schottky; 1.8–3.3 V for an LED).
- **Reverse biased**: it blocks, up to its reverse voltage rating.

A meter's **diode test** shows about 0.5–0.7 V one way and OL the other. OL both ways: open. Near 0 both ways: short.

**Rectifiers** turn AC into DC. The peak of AC is $\sqrt{2}$ times its RMS value: 12 V RMS peaks at about 17 V.

- **Half-wave** (one diode): uses one half of each cycle; peak out = peak in − 0.7 V.
- **Bridge** (four diodes): uses both halves, two diodes in series each time, so peak out = peak in − 1.4 V. The ripple is at **twice** the supply frequency: 100 Hz from 50 Hz.

A **smoothing capacitor** fills the gaps. Ripple: $\Delta V \approx \frac{I}{fC}$, with $f$ the ripple frequency.

Series resistor for an **LED** (or a **zener**): $R = \frac{V_s - V_f}{I}$.

A **zener** is made to break down at a set reverse voltage, so it holds that voltage: a simple reference or clamp.

A **flyback** (freewheel) diode goes across a DC coil, **pointing against the supply** (band to +). At switch-off the coil's current keeps flowing round through it, instead of making a spike of hundreds of volts that would damage the transistor or burn the contact. Fitted the wrong way, it is a short circuit across the supply.

formulas.name: Peak from RMS
formulas.says: A sine wave's peak is about 1.414 times its RMS value, the value a meter shows on AC.
symbols: the RMS voltage, as a meter reads it (V)

formulas.name: Bridge rectifier output peak
formulas.says: Two silicon diodes conduct at a time in a bridge, each dropping about 0.7 V.
symbols: the peak of the rectified output (V)
the peak of the AC going in (V)
formulas.example: 17.0 V peak in: about 15.6 V peak out.

formulas.name: Series resistor for an LED or zener
formulas.says: The resistor takes whatever voltage the diode does not, at the current you want.
symbols: the diode's forward voltage, or the zener voltage (V)
formulas.example: 24 V supply, a 2 V LED at 10 mA: $\frac{24 - 2}{0.010} = 2200$ Ω.

formulas.name: Ripple after a smoothing capacitor
formulas.says: Between peaks the capacitor alone feeds the load and its voltage sags. The bigger the capacitor and the more often it is topped up, the smaller the sag.
symbols: the ripple frequency (Hz): 100 Hz for a bridge on 50 Hz, 50 Hz for half-wave
formulas.example: 0.5 A from a bridge with 4700 µF: $\frac{0.5}{100 \times 0.0047} \approx 1.1$ V.

bench.task: Test three diodes with your multimeter's diode-test range: a 1N4007 (or any rectifier diode), an LED and a spare relay's freewheel diode. Unpowered parts only.
check: Red lead on the anode, black on the band (cathode): note the reading (about 0.5–0.7 V for silicon)
Swap the leads: OL means it blocks
The LED may glow faintly on diode test and read about 1.6–2.5 V
OL both ways means open; near 0 both ways means shorted

bench.task: Light an LED from a 12 V DC bench supply through the resistor you worked out for 10 mA (1 kΩ is close). 12 V DC only.
check: Work out $R = \frac{12 - 2}{0.010}$ before you wire it
Band (the LED's flat side, shorter leg) towards 0 V
Measure across the resistor and work out the current: V ÷ R
Turn the LED round: it goes out and nothing is harmed

cards.q: A silicon diode is in series with a 12 V DC lamp, and the lamp is lit. You turn the diode round. What happens?
options: The lamp goes out
The lamp stays lit at the same brightness
The lamp glows at half brightness
The diode shorts and blows the fuse
cards.why: Turned round, the diode is reverse biased and blocks: no current, no light. Half brightness is what a diode does on AC, where it passes one half of each cycle.

cards.title: A one-way valve for current
cards.body:
A **diode** lets current flow from its **anode** to its **cathode**, and not back. The cathode is the end with the **band**.

- **Forward biased** (anode more positive than cathode): it conducts, once the voltage across it passes its **forward voltage**, about **0.7 V** for silicon.
- **Reverse biased**: it blocks, up to its reverse voltage rating. Past that it breaks down.

While conducting, the drop stays near 0.7 V whatever the current, within its rating.
cards.more:
A non-return valve in a water pipe opens when the pressure pushes it the right way, and only once there is enough pressure to lift the flap. Pushed the other way, it slams shut.

A silicon diode's 'flap' needs about 0.6–0.7 V to open. Below that, almost nothing flows. Above it, the current is set by the rest of the circuit, and the diode just takes its 0.7 V.

Other kinds open at other voltages: a **Schottky** at about 0.2–0.4 V (less wasted heat, used in power supplies), an **LED** at about 1.8 V (red) to 3.3 V (blue or white).

cards.q: On a diode's body, what does the band mark?
options: The cathode: current flows out of this end
The anode: current flows into this end
Its voltage rating, by the band's colour
The end that must go to earth
cards.why: The band is the cathode, the bar in the symbol. Conventional current flows anode to cathode, so out of the banded end when it conducts.

cards.title: Testing a diode with a meter
cards.body:
A multimeter's **diode test** passes a small current and shows the voltage across the part.

- Red on the anode, black on the cathode: a good silicon diode reads about **0.5–0.7 V**.
- Swapped: **OL** (it blocks).
- **OL both ways**: the diode is open.
- **Near 0 V both ways**: it is shorted.

Test diodes out of circuit, or at least with the power off: other parts in parallel can fool the reading.
cards.more:
The meter is a tiny battery with a current limit. Forward, the diode opens and the meter shows the voltage it takes to do so, the forward voltage, about 0.6 V. Reverse, nothing flows and the meter runs out of range: OL.

A bridge rectifier is four diodes, so test it as four: from each AC terminal to + (one way conducts), and from − to each AC terminal. A shorted bridge diode usually blows the fuse; an open one halves the ripple frequency and makes the DC sag under load.

cards.q: A rectifier diode reads 0.002 V on diode test one way and 0.002 V the other. What is wrong?
options: It is shorted
It is open circuit
Nothing: that is a good diode
The meter's battery is flat
cards.why: A good diode reads about 0.6 V one way and OL the other. Near zero both ways means current flows freely both ways: a short. Open would read OL both ways.

cards.title: Rectifiers: AC in, DC out
cards.body:
AC swings both ways. Its **peak** is $\sqrt{2}$ (about 1.414) times the **RMS** value a meter shows.

- **Half-wave**: one diode. Only the positive halves get through. Peak out = peak in − 0.7 V.
- **Bridge**: four diodes. Both halves come out positive. Two diodes conduct at a time, so peak out = peak in − 1.4 V. The output bumps up **twice** per cycle: 100 times a second on 50 Hz.

The bridge is what is in nearly every DC power supply.
cards.more:
Numbers first. A transformer gives 12 V RMS. Its peak is $12 \times 1.414 = 17.0$ V.

Half-wave: the positive humps get through, less 0.7 V: humps 16.3 V high, with gaps between them where the negative halves were. The bumps come 50 times a second.

Bridge: the diodes steer both halves the same way, so there are no gaps, just humps back to back, each 17.0 − 1.4 = 15.6 V high, 100 times a second. Two diodes at 0.7 V each are in the path on every half-cycle, which is where the 1.4 V goes.

Without a capacitor, the output is lumpy DC: always positive, never steady.

cards.q: A transformer gives {vr} V RMS into a bridge rectifier. What is the peak of the DC output?
cards.work: $V_{pk} = \sqrt{2} \times {vr} = {vp_show}$ V; less 1.4 V for two diodes: {answer} V
cards.why: RMS to peak first (× 1.414), then take off two diode drops. Forgetting the √2 gives a figure well under the real one.
cards.hint: Peak = RMS × √2. A bridge has two diodes in the path at a time.

cards.q: A bridge rectifier runs from the 50 Hz supply. At what frequency is the ripple on its output?
options: 100 Hz
50 Hz
25 Hz
150 Hz
cards.why: A bridge turns both halves of each cycle into a positive hump: two humps per cycle, 100 a second. Half-wave gives one a cycle, 50 Hz. A bridge humming at 50 Hz usually has one diode open.

cards.title: Smoothing: a capacitor fills the gaps
cards.body:
A large **capacitor** across the output charges up to the peak on each hump. Between humps it alone feeds the load, and its voltage sags a little: the **ripple**.

$$\Delta V \approx \frac{I}{fC}$$

$\Delta V$ is the ripple (volts), $I$ the load current (amps), $f$ the **ripple** frequency (100 Hz for a bridge on 50 Hz), $C$ the capacitance in **farads** (1000 µF = 0.001 F).

More current, more ripple; a bigger capacitor or a bridge, less.
cards.more:
The capacitor is a bucket that a tap tops up in short bursts, while a hole in the bottom (the load) drains it steadily. Between bursts the level drops.

How far it drops depends on how fast it drains (the current), how big the bucket is (the capacitance), and how often it is topped up (the ripple frequency).

Example: 1 A load, 4700 µF, bridge on 50 Hz: $\frac{1}{100 \times 0.0047} = 2.1$ V of ripple. Double the capacitor to 10 000 µF and it roughly halves. A regulator after it (such as a 7812 for 12 V) then takes out the rest, as long as the troughs stay a couple of volts above its output.

cards.q: A bridge rectifier on 50 Hz feeds {i} A into a load, smoothed by a {c} µF capacitor. Roughly how much ripple is there?
cards.why: A bridge on 50 Hz tops the capacitor up 100 times a second, so f = 100 Hz. µF × $10^{-6}$ is farads.
cards.hint: Ripple frequency for a bridge on 50 Hz: 100 Hz. Capacitance in farads.

cards.title: LEDs and zeners need a resistor
cards.body:
An **LED** drops about 2 V (red) to 3 V (blue, white) and wants about 5–20 mA. Wired straight across 24 V it would draw far too much and die. A **series resistor** takes the rest of the voltage:

$$R = \frac{V_s - V_f}{I}$$

$V_s$ is the supply, $V_f$ the LED's forward voltage, $I$ the current you want, in amps.

A **zener** diode is used **reverse** biased: it breaks down at a set voltage (5.1 V, 12 V…) and holds it, so it makes a simple reference. It needs a series resistor the same way.
cards.more:
The resistor and the LED share the supply. The LED takes its 2 V whatever happens, so the resistor must take the other 22 V of a 24 V supply. Pick the current, say 10 mA = 0.010 A, and Ohm's law gives the resistor: $22 \div 0.010 = 2200$ Ω. Pick the nearest standard value, 2.2 kΩ.

Check the resistor's power too: $P = VI = 22 \times 0.010 = 0.22$ W, so a 0.25 W resistor is cutting it fine; use 0.5 W.

A zener works like a pressure relief valve: below its voltage it does nothing; at its voltage it conducts as much as it must to stop the voltage rising further. The resistor limits how much that is.

cards.q: An LED with a forward voltage of {vf} V is to run at {ma} mA from a {vs} V supply. What series resistor does it need?
cards.why: The resistor takes the supply less the LED's drop, at the current you chose. mA ÷ 1000 is amps.
cards.hint: Voltage across the resistor = supply − LED voltage. Then R = V ÷ I, with I in amps.

cards.title: The diode across a relay coil
cards.body:
A coil (a relay, a contactor, a solenoid valve) **resists any sudden change of current**. Switch it off and it drives the current on for a moment, making a reverse spike of **hundreds of volts** that can kill the transistor in a PLC output or burn a contact.

A **flyback** (freewheel) diode across the coil, **pointing against the supply** (band to +), does nothing in normal running: it is reverse biased. At switch-off, the coil's current loops round through it and dies away harmlessly.
cards.more:
Think of water flowing fast through a long pipe. Slam a valve shut and the water's momentum makes a pressure spike: water hammer. A coil's magnetic field is that momentum for current.

The diode gives the current somewhere to go: round and round through the coil and diode until the energy is spent as a little heat. The spike is held to about 0.7 V above the supply.

The price is that the relay drops out a few milliseconds more slowly. If that matters, a diode plus a zener in series, or a varistor, lets the field collapse faster.

On AC coils a diode cannot be used (it would conduct every other half-cycle): there you use an RC snubber or a varistor.

cards.q: Why is a diode fitted across a 24 V DC relay coil, band towards +24 V?
options: To give the coil's current a path at switch-off
To stop the relay chattering when it is on
To rectify the supply for the relay coil
To light the relay's indicator when it is on
cards.why: In normal running the diode is reverse biased and does nothing. At switch-off, the coil drives its current on through the diode instead of making a spike that would damage the transistor or contact switching it.

cards.q: A 230 V to 18 V transformer feeds a bridge rectifier and a 4700 µF capacitor. The load takes 1 A. What is the DC at its peaks, and how low do the troughs go?

steps.ask: The ripple, with a bridge on 50 Hz.

cards.why: Peak from RMS, take off the diodes, then the ripple. The troughs matter: a regulator after this must have its output a couple of volts below 22 V to keep working.

cards.q: A {vr} V RMS supply goes through a single diode (half-wave) into a {c} µF capacitor feeding {i} A. Roughly how much ripple is there?
cards.work: Half-wave tops up 50 times a second: $\frac{{i}}{50 \times {c} \times 10^{-6}} = {answer}$ V
cards.why: One hump per cycle, so f = 50 Hz, and the ripple is twice what a bridge would give. The RMS voltage does not come into the ripple at all: it is there to tempt you.
cards.hint: How often does a half-wave rectifier top the capacitor up on 50 Hz?

cards.q: A {vz} V zener is to hold a reference from a {vs} V supply, with {ma} mA through it. What series resistor?
cards.why: Same rule as an LED: the resistor takes the difference between the supply and the zener's voltage. (Any load on the reference takes some of that current too: in real designs add the load current.)
cards.hint: Voltage across the resistor is the supply minus the zener voltage.

cards.q: A new 24 V DC solenoid valve keeps blowing its 1 A fuse the moment it is switched on. One line of the description is the fault. Which?
lines: PLC output Q0.3 switches +24 V to the coil's terminal A1
The coil's terminal A2 goes to 0 V
A 1N4007 diode is across the coil: band to A2 (0 V), plain end to A1
The coil draws 0.3 A when on
cards.fix: Band (cathode) to A1, the +24 V end; plain end (anode) to A2, the 0 V end
cards.why: Fitted band to 0 V, the diode is forward biased across the supply: a short circuit the moment the output turns on. A flyback diode always points against the supply, so it is reverse biased in normal running. Check: with the coil on, the diode should have 24 V across it the blocking way.

cards.q: A silicon diode in a supply carries {i} A. Roughly how much power does it turn into heat?
cards.why: Power is voltage times current, and a conducting silicon diode takes about 0.7 V. At several amps that is real heat: bridges for big currents bolt to a heatsink. A Schottky's lower drop wastes less.
cards.hint: $P = VI$, with V the diode's forward drop.

cards.q: Someone wires a red LED straight across a 24 V DC supply, with no resistor. What happens?
options: It flashes bright and dies
It lights normally
It glows dimly
Nothing: an LED only needs 2 V
cards.why: With nothing to limit it, the current through a conducting diode is set only by the supply's limit and the wiring: far past the LED's 20 mA. A resistor must take the other 22 V. Indicator lamps built for 24 V have the resistor inside.

cards.q: A meter reads {vr} V AC (RMS). What is the peak?
cards.why: Meters show RMS; the waveform's peak is 1.414 times higher. That is why a capacitor on rectified 230 V charges to about 325 V, and a diode's reverse rating must be well above that.

cards.q: A {vr} V RMS supply goes through a single diode (half-wave). What is the peak of the output?
cards.why: One diode in the path, so one 0.7 V drop. A bridge has two in the path at a time (1.4 V). Which rectifier is it?
cards.hint: How many diodes is the current going through?

cards.q: A bridge rectifier's DC output hums at 50 Hz instead of 100 Hz, and sags under load. What is the likely fault?
options: One diode in the bridge is open
One diode in the bridge is shorted
The smoothing capacitor is too large
The transformer's output is too high
cards.why: With one diode open, one half of each cycle is lost: the bridge works like a half-wave rectifier, with ripple at 50 Hz and twice as large. A shorted diode usually blows the fuse instead.

cards.q: Match each job with which way the diode is biased while it does it.
pairs: A rectifier diode passing the positive half-cycle
A flyback diode while the coil is on
cards.why: Most diodes work forward. A zener is made to work in reverse breakdown. A flyback diode sits reverse biased until the switch-off spike turns it forward.

cards.q: A diode is in series with a 24 V DC relay coil, band towards the 0 V end, and the relay works. You turn the diode round. What happens?
options: The relay drops out
The relay stays in
The relay chatters
The fuse blows
cards.why: In series, the diode was forward biased and passing the coil's current. Turned round, it blocks, so the coil gets nothing. In series a diode can only pass or block; across a coil, the wrong way round, it would short the supply.

cards.q: A bridge rectifier is fed {vr} V RMS. What is the peak DC output?
cards.why: Peak from RMS (× 1.414), less two diode drops.

cards.q: A 2 V LED is to run at 10 mA from {vs} V. What series resistor?
cards.why: Supply less the LED's drop, divided by the current in amps.

cards.q: Match each part with its job.
pairs: Turns both halves of AC into positive humps
Holds a fixed voltage when reverse biased
